This PR enables overlap only for FDFO + LowConfidence. FDFO executes one forward pass and one denoise step per `run_batch()`, requiring frequent scheduling. Sync mode completes multiple denoise steps within one `run_batch()`, amortizing scheduling overhead; overlap is not currently supported for sync mode. Related to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39499 # Design ## Asynchronous run_batch() Overlap scheduling requires the scheduler to submit `run_batch()` and continue without waiting for GPU results. Some existing paths frequently synchronize the scheduler with the GPU. These paths need to return GPU tensors first and defer CPU consumption. For example, FDFO's `LowConfidence.step()` updates tokens and computes completion flags directly on GPU tensors, without calling `.tolist()` or reading GPU booleans inside the step. `DllmRunOutput.block_tokens` and `block_done` both remain tensors. ## Dependencies between batches Overlap requires the scheduler to schedule batch N+1 before receiving batch N's results. At that point, the CPU has not processed batch N's results. However, the next forward pass must use the updated block tokens from the previous step, rather than the CPU inputs that have not yet been updated. FutureMap adds `dllm_block_tokens_buf`, which stores a full block of tokens per request slot. After batch N's step, it writes the tokens into the corresponding row. Before its forward pass, N+1 reads that row and replaces its block input. This dependency stays on the GPU without passing through CPU result processing. Each row starts at `-1`, indicating that no result is available. A new block's first execution keeps the input prepared by the scheduler; FutureMap replaces it only when the row is valid. Block handoff and request completion clear the old row to `-1`, preventing the next block or a new request from reading stale tokens. `result.dllm_algo_state` retains the interface for returning algorithm state, but that state is not forwarded through FutureMap to the next step submitted ahead of result processing. Overlap for general stateful algorithms requires further adaptation. ## Request and resource lifecycle An FDFO request proceeds through block preparation, denoising, block handoff, and request completion. A request may contain multiple blocks. Both `req` and its request slot are retained across block transitions; the slot is released only when the request finishes or is aborted. ```mermaid flowchart TD S(["Request arrives"]) --> A["Prepare a new block
prepare_for_extend()"] A --> B["One denoise step
_run_fdfo()"] B --> C{"Process a valid result
Block complete?"} C -->|Complete| D{"Commit output
Request finished?"} D -->|Finished| F["Clear FutureMap and release resources
release_kv_cache()"] F --> T(["Request ends"]) C -->|Incomplete: retain slot / KV| B D -->|Continue generating| E["Hand off the current block
get_next_batch_to_run()"] E --> A ``` ### Resource handoff driven by block state #### State and transitions | Field | Meaning and purpose | |---|---| | GPU `done` returned by `step()` | Per-block completion flag. Returned through `DllmRunOutput.block_done` → `result.dllm_block_done` and consumed once the result is readable on the CPU; not stored in FutureMap. | | `req.dllm_block_done` | Set to `True` for an accepted completion result; prompt-only blocks can set it early during preparation. Reset to `False` after a new block is admitted. | | `req.dllm_block_id` | ID of the current block. Incremented when `prepare_for_extend()` opens a new block; unchanged within a block. | | `result.dllm_block_ids` | An immutable tuple captured when a batch is submitted. Each entry snapshots the corresponding request's block ID; result processing compares it with the current ID to identify stale results. | GPU `done=True` means that this forward pass has computed KV for the final tokens. LowConfidence checks completion before updating tokens, so the step that fills the last mask still returns `False`; another forward pass is needed to complete the block. CPU-side `dllm_block_done` records whether the scheduler has accepted that completion result. These are separate states. ### Block advancement and resource handoff **Handing off the old block** and **opening a new block** are separate stages, each performed once: ```text Prepare the batch → If the block is prompt-only, mark done=True early → Submit GPU execution Start the next scheduling iteration → Hand off the old block: hand off completed KV and clear FutureMap → Retain the old block ID, done=True, and request slot Check resources in the adder ├─ Insufficient: keep waiting └─ Sufficient: enter prepare_for_extend() Open a new block: block ID + 1, done=False ``` Denoise steps within a block reuse its KV allocation. At handoff, completed KV is passed to the prefix-cache manager. The request slot is retained across blocks and released only on completion or abort. FutureMap clearing runs after the old GPU writeback and before the new block reads the row, ordered by the forward stream. #### 1. Avoid scheduling a prompt block twice If `done` is set only during result processing, overlap scheduling still sees the current prompt block as incomplete when preparing the next batch and schedules the same forward pass again. Instead, at the end of `prepare_for_extend()`, a block entirely within the prompt is marked `done=True` early. The next scheduling iteration knows that it needs only one forward pass and can advance without waiting for result processing. Here, `done` means that scheduling can advance; it does not mean GPU execution has finished. The current batch still executes its forward pass to compute KV. Mixed blocks and decode blocks containing positions to generate still require a valid completion result. #### 2. Avoid repeated handoff while waiting for resources At the start of scheduling, hand off only completed blocks that have not yet been handed off: ```python if req.dllm_block_done and req.extend_end > req.prefix_len: # Clear FutureMap and hand off the current block's KV. ``` Handoff leaves `prefix_len == extend_end`. Even if resources remain insufficient for several iterations, handoff is not repeated. While waiting, the next block is not initialized, and the old block ID and `done=True` remain unchanged. Only requests actually added to the batch reach `prepare_for_extend()`, which initializes the new block, increments its ID, and resets `done`. `NO_TOKEN` can also mean that the current request joined the batch but exhausted the remaining budget, so this return value alone does not indicate whether admission succeeded. Late results from the old block are rejected by `done=True` while waiting, and by the block ID mismatch after the new block opens. This prevents duplicate output commits and updates to the new block's state. In sync mode, one `_run_sync()` completes the current block, and `done` is set after it returns. The request slot is likewise retained if generation continues. ## Resource reuse At block handoff, request completion, or abort, resources are reused as follows: - **Request slot:** Retain the ReqToTokenPool row across blocks. Return it for reuse by another request only on completion or abort. The WAR barrier orders subsequent scheduler writes to the shared mapping after the old forward pass has finished reading it. - **KV pages:** Valid prefix KV may remain in the radix cache for reuse; the rest is reclaimed according to the cache policy. Old and new forward passes execute in order on the same forward stream. Even if the CPU has reassigned page indices, new computation cannot overwrite KV still in use by the old computation. - **FutureMap:** Clear the row at block handoff, and before returning the slot on completion or abort. Enqueue the clear to `-1` on the forward stream. It executes after the old denoise round's last writeback and before the new forward pass reads the row, preventing stale tokens from leaking into the next block or a new request. **Returning resource indices on the CPU** and **accessing those resources on the GPU** are separate operations. The CPU can reclaim and reassign indices before the old GPU work finishes, while stream dependencies order GPU accesses without requiring the CPU to wait for the entire round. Late CPU results are discarded through the finished, block ID, and block-done checks, preventing duplicate output commits or resource releases. ## Extra denoise cancellation ### LowConfidence: avoid redundant forwards before submission After LowConfidence fills the last mask, one final forward pass is still required to write KV for the final tokens. The scheduler uses the CPU-side `dllm_incomplete_ids` and `result_queue` to determine whether this forward pass has already been submitted, without an additional read of GPU `done`. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Schedule the current request"] --> B{"CPU block tokens nonempty and mask-free?"} B -->|No| C["Schedule denoising normally"] B -->|Yes| D{"Request in result_queue?"} D -->|No| E["Schedule the final forward to refresh KV"] D -->|Yes| F["Final forward already in flight
Skip duplicate scheduling"] E --> G["Process a valid completion result
Commit output and set block_done"] F --> G ``` This preserves the required KV refresh while avoiding another redundant forward pass. Skipping scheduling does not set `dllm_block_done` early or open a new block; a valid completion result is still required. ### Other algorithms: rely on completion signals and filter late results Other algorithms may continue processing mask-free blocks, so LowConfidence's early check does not apply. **Overlap remains disabled for these algorithms.** Future support must use each algorithm's completion semantics to determine whether scheduling can stop early. The general result-filtering path remains in place and also handles cases such as aborted LowConfidence requests. `process_batch_result_dllm()` checks result validity before consuming the completion state returned by the algorithm: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Process a batch result"] --> B{"Request finished, block ID mismatch,
or current block_done=True?"} B -->|Yes| C["Discard the late or duplicate result"] B -->|No| D{"Algorithm returned done=True?"} D -->|No| E["Save intermediate state and continue denoising"] D -->|Yes| F["Commit output and set block_done"] ``` ```python if ( req.finished() or result.dllm_block_ids[i] != req.dllm_block_id or req.dllm_block_done ): continue ``` The block ID rejects old results after a new block opens; `block_done` rejects duplicate results after completion but before the next block opens; `finished` rejects results after request completion or abort. Discarding a result does not cancel already-submitted GPU work or save a forward pass. Already-submitted GPU work may still access KV and FutureMap. Clearing the corresponding row runs after the old work and before the next block or a new request reads it. CUDA stream ordering ensures safe reuse without requiring the CPU to wait for the entire round. ## Prompt block handling At the end of `prepare_for_extend()`, a prompt-only block is marked complete early: ```python if req.extend_end <= len(req.origin_input_ids): req.dllm_block_done = True ``` The current block still executes one forward pass to compute KV. The early flag lets the next scheduling iteration advance without waiting for result processing. The old block hands off resources at the start of that iteration; the next input is initialized and the ID advances only after admission succeeds. The flag does not mean that GPU execution has finished; stream ordering still enforces GPU dependencies. Decode blocks containing positions to generate, including mixed blocks that cross the prompt boundary, do not take this shortcut. A new block starts with `dllm_block_done=False` and cannot open the next block until a valid completion result is processed. For LowConfidence, duplicate scheduling is paused while the final forward pass is in flight. ## Request abort handling Aborting a request requires both invalidating old results and clearing stale data in its slot. The finished flag prevents late results from modifying the request. `_clear_dllm_future()` prevents a new request from reading the old block when it reuses the slot. Clearing must run after the old GPU work's final stash; otherwise, that work could write stale data back into the cleared row. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["abort_request()"] --> B["Remove from scheduling queues and mark finished"] B --> C["_clear_dllm_future()"] C --> D["release_kv_cache()"] D --> E["New request reuses the slot"] B -. Late result .-> F["req.finished() → skip"] ``` The diagram shows the CPU call order. The forward stream and scheduler stream dependencies enforce safe GPU ordering without requiring the CPU to wait for the entire extra denoise round. # Performance > 2026-10-15: Both main columns in the performance table use PR base `121aa8dcc7`; the PR workspace is based on `19d6a491a2`. Both main columns were rerun; the three PR columns retain the measurements from the same day. The main baseline for correctness and profiling below remains `a776851c97`. Hi @rwang5203, this PR is now ready for review.
Could you take a look and help trigger CI? Thanks!

Thanks for the detailed design notes, they made the block lifecycle easy to follow. I compared this branch with main on one H200 using LLaDA2.0-mini, the default `--dllm-algorithm LowConfidence` launch plus `--max-running-requests 16`, 128 input and 128 output tokens, and fresh servers in alternating order. At concurrency 1 output throughput improves about 22%, GSM8K is unchanged, and cancelling live streams under overlap left the server healthy. At concurrency 16 throughput drops about 12% with overlap, about 25% with `--disable-overlap-schedule`, and about 20% with `--no-dllm-fdfo`, and the logs trace this to the phase refresh in the first comment, because that run repeats earlier prompts and hits the prefix cache. With phases refreshed before grouping, overlap beats main by about 17% at concurrency 16 and overlap off matches main, so the scheduling approach holds up well once that is fixed.

Thanks for pointing this out. I revisit how we schedule the next batch under overlap.
Now our overlap don't scheduler any redundant forward.

For  LowConfidence, we have an early signal: **once a block contains no mask tokens, it needs only one final forward to refresh its KV cache.** We can use this to avoid submitting the redundant forward, instead of executing it and discarding its result.

However other algorithms may continue denoising a fully unmasked block, so “no masks” is not a general dLLM completion signal. Considering other algorithm, we still need block id to discard redundant result.

detail.body:
This PR enables overlap only for FDFO + LowConfidence. FDFO executes one forward pass and one denoise step per `run_batch()`, requiring frequent scheduling. Sync mode completes multiple denoise steps within one `run_batch()`, amortizing scheduling overhead; overlap is not currently supported for sync mode. Related to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39499 # Design ## Asynchronous run_batch() Overlap scheduling requires the scheduler to submit `run_batch()` and continue without waiting for GPU results. Some existing paths frequently synchronize the scheduler with the GPU. These paths need to return GPU tensors first and defer CPU consumption. For example, FDFO's `LowConfidence.step()` updates tokens and computes completion flags directly on GPU tensors, without calling `.tolist()` or reading GPU booleans inside the step. `DllmRunOutput.block_tokens` and `block_done` both remain tensors. ## Dependencies between batches Overlap requires the scheduler to schedule batch N+1 before receiving batch N's results. At that point, the CPU has not processed batch N's results. However, the next forward pass must use the updated block tokens from the previous step, rather than the CPU inputs that have not yet been updated. FutureMap adds `dllm_block_tokens_buf`, which stores a full block of tokens per request slot. After batch N's step, it writes the tokens into the corresponding row. Before its forward pass, N+1 reads that row and replaces its block input. This dependency stays on the GPU without passing through CPU result processing. Each row starts at `-1`, indicating that no result is available. A new block's first execution keeps the input prepared by the scheduler; FutureMap replaces it only when the row is valid. Block handoff and request completion clear the old row to `-1`, preventing the next block or a new request from reading stale tokens. `result.dllm_algo_state` retains the interface for returning algorithm state, but that state is not forwarded through FutureMap to the next step submitted ahead of result processing. Overlap for general stateful algorithms requires further adaptation. ## Request and resource lifecycle An FDFO request proceeds through block preparation, denoising, block handoff, and request completion. A request may contain multiple blocks. Both `req` and its request slot are retained across block transitions; the slot is released only when the request finishes or is aborted. ```mermaid flowchart TD S(["Request arrives"]) --> A["Prepare a new block
prepare_for_extend()"] A --> B["One denoise step
_run_fdfo()"] B --> C{"Process a valid result
Block complete?"} C -->|Complete| D{"Commit output
Request finished?"} D -->|Finished| F["Clear FutureMap and release resources
release_kv_cache()"] F --> T(["Request ends"]) C -->|Incomplete: retain slot / KV| B D -->|Continue generating| E["Hand off the current block
get_next_batch_to_run()"] E --> A ``` ### Resource handoff driven by block state #### State and transitions | Field | Meaning and purpose | |---|---| | GPU `done` returned by `step()` | Per-block completion flag. Returned through `DllmRunOutput.block_done` → `result.dllm_block_done` and consumed once the result is readable on the CPU; not stored in FutureMap. | | `req.dllm_block_done` | Set to `True` for an accepted completion result; prompt-only blocks can set it early during preparation. Reset to `False` after a new block is admitted. | | `req.dllm_block_id` | ID of the current block. Incremented when `prepare_for_extend()` opens a new block; unchanged within a block. | | `result.dllm_block_ids` | An immutable tuple captured when a batch is submitted. Each entry snapshots the corresponding request's block ID; result processing compares it with the current ID to identify stale results. | GPU `done=True` means that this forward pass has computed KV for the final tokens. LowConfidence checks completion before updating tokens, so the step that fills the last mask still returns `False`; another forward pass is needed to complete the block. CPU-side `dllm_block_done` records whether the scheduler has accepted that completion result. These are separate states. ### Block advancement and resource handoff **Handing off the old block** and **opening a new block** are separate stages, each performed once: ```text Prepare the batch → If the block is prompt-only, mark done=True early → Submit GPU execution Start the next scheduling iteration → Hand off the old block: hand off completed KV and clear FutureMap → Retain the old block ID, done=True, and request slot Check resources in the adder ├─ Insufficient: keep waiting └─ Sufficient: enter prepare_for_extend() Open a new block: block ID + 1, done=False ``` Denoise steps within a block reuse its KV allocation. At handoff, completed KV is passed to the prefix-cache manager. The request slot is retained across blocks and released only on completion or abort. FutureMap clearing runs after the old GPU writeback and before the new block reads the row, ordered by the forward stream. #### 1. Avoid scheduling a prompt block twice If `done` is set only during result processing, overlap scheduling still sees the current prompt block as incomplete when preparing the next batch and schedules the same forward pass again. Instead, at the end of `prepare_for_extend()`, a block entirely within the prompt is marked `done=True` early. The next scheduling iteration knows that it needs only one forward pass and can advance without waiting for result processing. Here, `done` means that scheduling can advance; it does not mean GPU execution has finished. The current batch still executes its forward pass to compute KV. Mixed blocks and decode blocks containing positions to generate still require a valid completion result. #### 2. Avoid repeated handoff while waiting for resources At the start of scheduling, hand off only completed blocks that have not yet been handed off: ```python if req.dllm_block_done and req.extend_end > req.prefix_len: # Clear FutureMap and hand off the current block's KV. ``` Handoff leaves `prefix_len == extend_end`. Even if resources remain insufficient for several iterations, handoff is not repeated. While waiting, the next block is not initialized, and the old block ID and `done=True` remain unchanged. Only requests actually added to the batch reach `prepare_for_extend()`, which initializes the new block, increments its ID, and resets `done`. `NO_TOKEN` can also mean that the current request joined the batch but exhausted the remaining budget, so this return value alone does not indicate whether admission succeeded. Late results from the old block are rejected by `done=True` while waiting, and by the block ID mismatch after the new block opens. This prevents duplicate output commits and updates to the new block's state. In sync mode, one `_run_sync()` completes the current block, and `done` is set after it returns. The request slot is likewise retained if generation continues. ## Resource reuse At block handoff, request completion, or abort, resources are reused as follows: - **Request slot:** Retain the ReqToTokenPool row across blocks. Return it for reuse by another request only on completion or abort. The WAR barrier orders subsequent scheduler writes to the shared mapping after the old forward pass has finished reading it. - **KV pages:** Valid prefix KV may remain in the radix cache for reuse; the rest is reclaimed according to the cache policy. Old and new forward passes execute in order on the same forward stream. Even if the CPU has reassigned page indices, new computation cannot overwrite KV still in use by the old computation. - **FutureMap:** Clear the row at block handoff, and before returning the slot on completion or abort. Enqueue the clear to `-1` on the forward stream. It executes after the old denoise round's last writeback and before the new forward pass reads the row, preventing stale tokens from leaking into the next block or a new request. **Returning resource indices on the CPU** and **accessing those resources on the GPU** are separate operations. The CPU can reclaim and reassign indices before the old GPU work finishes, while stream dependencies order GPU accesses without requiring the CPU to wait for the entire round. Late CPU results are discarded through the finished, block ID, and block-done checks, preventing duplicate output commits or resource releases. ## Extra denoise cancellation ### LowConfidence: avoid redundant forwards before submission After LowConfidence fills the last mask, one final forward pass is still required to write KV for the final tokens. The scheduler uses the CPU-side `dllm_incomplete_ids` and `result_queue` to determine whether this forward pass has already been submitted, without an additional read of GPU `done`. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Schedule the current request"] --> B{"CPU block tokens nonempty and mask-free?"} B -->|No| C["Schedule denoising normally"] B -->|Yes| D{"Request in result_queue?"} D -->|No| E["Schedule the final forward to refresh KV"] D -->|Yes| F["Final forward already in flight
Skip duplicate scheduling"] E --> G["Process a valid completion result
Commit output and set block_done"] F --> G ``` This preserves the required KV refresh while avoiding another redundant forward pass. Skipping scheduling does not set `dllm_block_done` early or open a new block; a valid completion result is still required. ### Other algorithms: rely on completion signals and filter late results Other algorithms may continue processing mask-free blocks, so LowConfidence's early check does not apply. **Overlap remains disabled for these algorithms.** Future support must use each algorithm's completion semantics to determine whether scheduling can stop early. The general result-filtering path remains in place and also handles cases such as aborted LowConfidence requests. `process_batch_result_dllm()` checks result validity before consuming the completion state returned by the algorithm: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Process a batch result"] --> B{"Request finished, block ID mismatch,
or current block_done=True?"} B -->|Yes| C["Discard the late or duplicate result"] B -->|No| D{"Algorithm returned done=True?"} D -->|No| E["Save intermediate state and continue denoising"] D -->|Yes| F["Commit output and set block_done"] ``` ```python if ( req.finished() or result.dllm_block_ids[i] != req.dllm_block_id or req.dllm_block_done ): continue ``` The block ID rejects old results after a new block opens; `block_done` rejects duplicate results after completion but before the next block opens; `finished` rejects results after request completion or abort. Discarding a result does not cancel already-submitted GPU work or save a forward pass. Already-submitted GPU work may still access KV and FutureMap. Clearing the corresponding row runs after the old work and before the next block or a new request reads it. CUDA stream ordering ensures safe reuse without requiring the CPU to wait for the entire round. ## Prompt block handling At the end of `prepare_for_extend()`, a prompt-only block is marked complete early: ```python if req.extend_end <= len(req.origin_input_ids): req.dllm_block_done = True ``` The current block still executes one forward pass to compute KV. The early flag lets the next scheduling iteration advance without waiting for result processing. The old block hands off resources at the start of that iteration; the next input is initialized and the ID advances only after admission succeeds. The flag does not mean that GPU execution has finished; stream ordering still enforces GPU dependencies. Decode blocks containing positions to generate, including mixed blocks that cross the prompt boundary, do not take this shortcut. A new block starts with `dllm_block_done=False` and cannot open the next block until a valid completion result is processed. For LowConfidence, duplicate scheduling is paused while the final forward pass is in flight. ## Request abort handling Aborting a request requires both invalidating old results and clearing stale data in its slot. The finished flag prevents late results from modifying the request. `_clear_dllm_future()` prevents a new request from reading the old block when it reuses the slot. Clearing must run after the old GPU work's final stash; otherwise, that work could write stale data back into the cleared row. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["abort_request()"] --> B["Remove from scheduling queues and mark finished"] B --> C["_clear_dllm_future()"] C --> D["release_kv_cache()"] D --> E["New request reuses the slot"] B -. Late result .-> F["req.finished() → skip"] ``` The diagram shows the CPU call order. The forward stream and scheduler stream dependencies enforce safe GPU ordering without requiring the CPU to wait for the entire extra denoise round. # Performance > 2026-10-15: Both main columns in the performance table use PR base `121aa8dcc7`; the PR workspace is based on `19d6a491a2`. Both main columns were rerun; the three PR columns retain the measurements from the same day. The main baseline for correctness and profiling below remains `a776851c97`. Each configuration uses a single H20, TP1, LLaDA2.0-mini, LowConfidence threshold 0.95, block/page sizes 4/16/32, with CUDA Graph and radix cache enabled. `max-running-requests=16`, `context-length=8192`, `mem-fraction-static=0.7`, seed 42. Thanks for pointing this out. I revisit how we schedule the next batch under overlap.
Now our overlap don't scheduler any redundant forward.

For  LowConfidence, we have an early signal: **once a block contains no mask tokens, it needs only one final forward to refresh its KV cache.** We can use this to avoid submitting the redundant forward, instead of executing it and discarding its result.

Thanks for the detailed design notes, they made the block lifecycle easy to follow. I compared this branch with main on one H200 using LLaDA2.0-mini, the default `--dllm-algorithm LowConfidence` launch plus `--max-running-requests 16`, 128 input and 128 output tokens, and fresh servers in alternating order. At concurrency 1 output throughput improves about 22%, GSM8K is unchanged, and cancelling live streams under overlap left the server healthy. At concurrency 16 throughput drops about 12% with overlap, about 25% with `--disable-overlap-schedule`, and about 20% with `--no-dllm-fdfo`, and the logs trace this to the phase refresh in the first comment, because that run repeats earlier prompts and hits the prefix cache. With phases refreshed before grouping, overlap beats main by about 17% at concurrency 16 and overlap off matches main, so the scheduling approach holds up well once that is fixed.
